about: Reference recordings of wild elk (Cervus canadensis), all from National Park Service sound libraries: Yellowstone National Park (sounds-elk page) and Rocky Mountain National Park (wildlife soundscapes page). Each library page says its recordings are in the public domain; licenses were checked on 2026-11-13. Yellowstone files co-credited to MSU Acoustic Atlas were left out (third party). trimStartSec/trimEndSec are seconds in the original MP3 as downloaded (audioUrl). Lead-in before the call is at least 0.3 s except where notes say otherwise. Calls were classified by measurement against the cited definitions in callDefinitions; uncertain clips say so in notes. No page says whether playback was used (playbackUsed null); the pages describe free-living elk and no human-made call is heard in the clips.

callDefinitions.readVia: Read directly on www.nps.gov on 2026-11-13 (the Yellowstone elk book as its PDF). rmef.org, state wildlife agency sites, academic.oup.com and en.wikipedia.org are blocked by this build environment's network, so the peer-reviewed papers the NPS book cites (Geist 2002; Feighny et al. 2006; Bowyer & Kitchen 1987) were not read; only the NPS text that cites them is used.

calls.name: Bugle
calls.definition: Bugles begin with a gradual increase in sound frequency and volume that rises to an extended squeal or whistle that ends abruptly and is often followed by a sequence of grunts or yelps (NPS Yellowstone elk book, citing Feighny et al. 2006). "A crescendo of deep, resonant tones that rise rapidly to a high-pitched squeal before dropping to a series of grunts" (NPS Rocky Mountain).
calls.use: Mature bulls bugle to attract mates and let other bulls know they will defend their group (harem) of females (elk book, citing Bowyer & Kitchen 1987); during the rut, early September to mid-October (NPS Yellowstone). Cows and younger bulls may also bugle, but cannot match the strength or range of older bulls (NPS Rocky Mountain).
calls.classifyBy: a rising tone into a sustained high whistle that ends abruptly, with or without grunts after.

calls.name: Glug
calls.definition: The "glug" sound a bull elk makes as he herds a harem of cows during the rut (NPS Rocky Mountain sound library). The elk book lists grunts among male vocalizations (citing Geist 2002).
calls.use: While a bull herds his harem of cows during the rut (NPS Rocky Mountain sound library).
calls.classifyBy: short low pulses in a series, in the recording the page labels as the glug.
calls.caveat: Only one recording; the source gives no acoustic description, so the clips are windows of that recording's pulse series.

calls.name: Cow mew
calls.definition: Mews are among the vocalizations of female elk, with chirps and whines (NPS Yellowstone elk book, citing Geist 2002). The Rocky Mountain sound library has a recording labelled the elk "mew" vocalization.
calls.use: Not stated in the sources read; no use is claimed here.
calls.classifyBy: short arched or descending tonal notes in the recording the page labels as mews, other than the long steady background bugles.
calls.caveat: The sources give no acoustic description of a mew; clips are classified by elimination and marked uncertain.

calls.name: Calf call
calls.definition: A call of an elk calf: the Yellowstone sound library's "Elk Calf" recording ("An elk calf calls out").
calls.use: Not stated in the sources read; no use is claimed here.
calls.classifyBy: the three calls in the recording the page labels as an elk calf calling.

clips.author: NPS / Neal Herbert
clips.licenseProof: The park's sound library page (licenseUrl) says its recordings are in the public domain and may be used without limitation, crediting the National Park Service.
clips.playbackNote: Not stated on the page. The page describes free-living elk in the park; no human-made call is heard in the clip.
clips.modifications: Trimmed; decoded from MP3 and converted to mono 44.1 kHz 16-bit WAV (stereo originals: channels averaged). No filtering or gain change.
clips.notes: Low tones (~0.6 and 1.2 kHz) from ~0.4 s, rising to a sustained whistle at ~1.9-2.0 kHz (~1.4-3.4 s) that ends abruptly with a falling sweep; then a series of grunts/yelps (~4.5-6.8 s). Matches the definition (rise, extended whistle ending abruptly, grunts after). Measured: SNR 40.2 dB (loudest 10 ms frame vs 10th-percentile frame, full band); peak sample 0.967 of full scale, no clipped samples. Original: Mammoth Hot Springs, Yellowstone National Park. Page: "a bull elk announces his availability and fitness to the group with a healthy bugle." Mono MP3, 44.1 kHz.
